scope: Theorem 5.1 (Periodic lattice memory) of the manuscript “Computation under Rapidly Vanishing Navier–Stokes Forcing” (preprints/Computation-under-Rapidly-Vanishing-Navier-Stokes-Forcing-September-27-2026/manuscript.pdf), one of the manuscripts of result family 376 of openai/math at commit 1581d4cbdd69. The statement is quoted verbatim from the text that pdftotext 24.02.0 (-raw -enc UTF-8) extracts from the PDF (SHA-256 931c07840228968b), with whitespace normalised, and was found there under this heading on PDF page 13. Text extraction flattens typeset mathematics (superscripts, subscripts, fractions, large operators, delimiters), so the quote can read differently from the typeset statement and can carry characters with no Unicode meaning; the PDF is authoritative. Finding the quote shows that the manuscript states it, not that it is true. AMVO has checked nothing about this claim.
statement: Fix a computable viscosity ν > 0. A finite deterministic machine and a finite input effectively determine a smooth force g on the unit flat torus T3 = (R/Z)3 with zero spatial mean. The Navier–Stokes equations with force g and zero initial velocity have a smooth solution (U, 0) with zero spatial mean. Its particle from a∗ = (1/4, 1/2, 1/2) enters the fixed open set O = {x ∈ T3 : 1/2 < x1 < 1 (mod 1)} at some finite time if and only if the machine halts on that input. For every pair of nonnegative integers r, J and every spatial multi-index α, there is an effective constant Cr,α,J such that ∥∂r t ∂α x U(t)∥∞ + ∥∂r t ∂α x g(t)∥∞ ≤ Cr,α,J (1 + t)−J , t ≥ 0. (35) There is also an effective smooth mean-zero solenoidal force f with the same bounds and exactly the same velocity and material event. It is f = g − ∇ϕ, with pressure −ϕ, where ϕ is the mean-zero periodic solution of ∆ϕ = div g. For either force, uniqueness holds among periodic classical solutions for which the velocity, its time derivative and its spatial derivatives through order two, and the pressure and its spatial gradient, are continuous on every [0, T] × T3. Pressure is normalized to have zero spatial mean.
